catalog_quote: In present-day ZZ, the situation is more complex in that the final vowels are deleted in connected-speech forms and surface as [a] prepausally and in citation forms. This has resulted in each monomorphemic word having two forms, monosyllabic in connected speech and disyllabic prepausally and in isolation. Although the connected-speech form is historically the more recent of the two, it is taken to be underlyingly basic in the synchronic phonology of the language. ... In common with other Zapotec languages, ZZ has both stress and tone; various observers have argued that tone and stress are independent of each other in Zapotec languages (Mock 1988, Sicoli 2007, Chávez Peón 2008). In ZZ, words are stressed on the penultimate syllable of their citation/prepausal form, which is the last syllable of their connected-speech/underlying form. ZZ contrasts three tones on the stressed syllable, high, mid and low; the majority of unstressed syllables are toneless. The low tone has a low type frequency in native morphemes. Clitics do not normally bear a distinctive tone ... [sec. 4.3] In present-day ZZ, stress uniformly falls on the penultimate syllable of the citation form. This stress assignment pattern continues the one reconstructed by Kaufman (1994-2007) for Proto-Zapotec

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fixed on the last syllable of the underlying/connected-speech word (the root syllable, Zapotec being prefixing with mostly monosyllabic roots); citation and pre-pausal forms add a paragogic [a] after that syllable (Table 4: /gid/ -> [gida] 'skin'), so in citation forms stress is uniformly penultimate. Tone (H/M/L) contrasts only on the stressed syllable; unstressed syllables mostly toneless.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. Clitics normally toneless (exceptions: plural =bí, 1SG =ã, respectful 3SG =mà bear tone); enclitics are outside the citation-form count implicitly (stress stays on the root syllable). Older (Stage 2) Spanish loans lose pretonic vowels; recent loans keep them, with Spanish stress mapped to ZZ tone (sec. 4.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; the author states the rule twice, once relative to citation/pre-pausal forms (penultimate, because of the paragogic [a]) and once relative to connected-speech/underlying forms (final). Reading 'fixed: final syllable' follows the underlying form; a catalog keyed to citation forms would enter 'fixed: penultimate syllable'. Language also has three contrastive tones restricted to the stressed syllable (tone language with a stress statement would be an alternative label).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Zaniza Zapotec (author's abbreviation ZZ), spoken in Santa María Zaniza, Sola de Vega district, Oaxaca = Glottolog zani1235 / ISO zpw (Papabuco branch); data from Operstein's own fieldwork. No dialect subdivision mentioned.

tone_statements.citation: Operstein, Natalie. 2004. Zaniza Zapotec phonology: synchronic and historical aspects. Paper presented at the SSILA annual meeting, Boston.
tone_statements.quote: 8(a). The stem of a stressable monosyllabic word has a high, mid, or low tone: High Mid Low lyéx ‘buzzard’ lyex ‘avocado’ ... ná ‘work’ na ‘today’ nà ‘thick’. ... 8(c). The epenthetic vowel of words ending in -a/-a’/-ã combines with the high or low tones of the stem vowel to produce phonetically long vowels with tones that are acoustically rising or falling ... 8(d). In words of more than one syllable only the stressed syllable bears distinctive tone: the syllables to the left (proclitics and initial syllables of polysyllabic Spanish loans) take the default mid
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (high, mid, low) contrast only on the stressed stem syllable; other syllables default mid; rising/falling phonetic (stem tone + mid epenthetic V); low rare; two clitics bear tone.

sources.locator: Sec. 2.1 'Zaniza Zapotec phonology', postprint ms p. 7 (p. 8); restated sec. 4.3, ms p. 22 (p. 23). Published pagination 211-238 not seen (postprint has author pagination).
sources.note: Sec. 2.1 'Zaniza Zapotec phonology' (ms p. 7): words are stressed on the penultimate syllable of the citation/prepausal form = last syllable of the connected-speech/underlying form; three tones (H, M, L) contrast only on the stressed syllable, most unstressed syllables toneless; clitics normally toneless. Sec. 4.3 (ms p. 22): 'stress uniformly falls on the penultimate syllable of the citation form', continuing the Proto-Zapotec pattern (Kaufman); pretonic vowels of Spanish loans lost in older loans.

sources.note: Family-level only: 'There is only one accent per phonological word, with phonological contrasts tending to neutralize in unstressed syllables' (ms p. 2); stress on the lexical (second) element of grammaticalizing two-element constructions (sec. 3). Cites Operstein 2015a (LINCOM) for Zaniza data; no Zaniza-specific stress rule.

sources.citation: Operstein, Natalie. 2021. The Peñafiel Vocabulary from San Juan Elotepec. Linguistic Discovery 17(1): 13-46. doi:10.1349/PS1.1537-0852.A.511
sources.note: About Elotepec primarily; for Zaniza: stress-conditioned split of Proto-Zapotec *t' (tap pretonically, /dʒ/ posttonically, Table 7) and posttonic vowels 'neutralize to an [a]-quality vowel in citation and pre-pausal forms and are dropped elsewhere' (p. 26, Table 13). Implies stress on the root syllable before the paragogic vowel; no explicit Zaniza stress rule.

sources.note: Likely (search snippet + the compilers note): sec. 3.2 restates that Zaniza Zapotec has three contrastive tones, high, mid and low, with low tone having the lowest type frequency in native vocabulary, and that Spanish loans receive a marked tone (early loans low; later loans high, more rarely mid) on the Spanish stressed syllable - tone as a loanword-marking device; no stress rule (per note 'Zaniza tones on loans only, no stress rule').

sources.note: Per Crossref abstract: analyses the 'unusual pattern of stress-to-tone mapping in early Spanish loanwords in Zaniza Zapotec' - loans assigned to a minority ('marked') prosodic pattern (early loans: Spanish stressed syllable -> the rare low tone; cf. 2004 handout 8f and 2016 IJAL) - and compares similar minority-pattern loan prosody elsewhere; presupposes the 3-tone (H/M/L on stressed syllable) system.
